children: Oil prices rose Tuesday as continued risks to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz kept Middle East supply concerns in focus, while investors awaited signs of diplomatic progress over the Iran conflict.
Brent crude futures rose 1.7% to $102.07 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate gained 1.7% to $97.4 a barrel in early European trading.

Oil markets remain caught between Middle East supply risks and prospects for diplomacy, according to Lukman Otunuga, head of market research at FXTM. Renewed escalation could push crude prices higher, while confirmation of direct U.S.-Iran talks at this week's United Nations General Assembly could weigh on prices by raising expectations for increased regional supply, he said. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has played down the prospect of talks taking place in New York, saying dialogue between the U.S. and Iran is essential but would probably take place elsewhere.

Shipping risks through Hormuz remain elevated. A tanker entering the strait was struck by a projectile on Monday, injuring two crew members, while another tanker was hit by debris, according to U.K. Maritime Trade Operations.

The incidents come even as energy traffic through Hormuz has increased. The volume of oil, natural gas and cargo passing through the strait over the past two weeks reached its highest level in six months, U.S. Central Command said.

Saudi Arabia is increasingly relying on Hormuz following the shutdown of its East-West Pipeline. Around 2.4 million barrels a day of Saudi crude and condensate flowed through the strait over the past two weeks, returning to levels last seen in early July, according to Kpler.

The four-week average of Saudi crude loadings from inside the Persian Gulf rose above 2 million barrels a day last week, from virtually zero for most of June and less than 1 million barrels a day in July, according to Vortexa.

Saudi Aramco is loading more crude at its Persian Gulf terminals and moving it through Hormuz before transferring some cargoes to tankers off Oman for delivery to customers. The company has told several Asian customers to pick up shipments off Oman, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

The increased reliance on ship-to-ship transfers is putting further pressure on tanker availability. Gulf of Oman ship-to-ship activity has surged to record levels, while capacity constraints could force more transfers toward western India or Malaysia, Kpler said.

Longer shuttle routes would sharply increase tanker requirements. Kpler estimates that redirecting 3 million barrels a day of Saudi crude would require an additional 36 to 40 very large crude carriers under its base case. Moving transfers as far as Malaysia could require as many as 58 VLCCs, compared with around 25 if the additional barrels were handled in the Gulf of Oman.

Transportation costs have already surged. The cost of shipping crude from Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura terminal to Ningbo in China has risen to nearly $63 million a voyage from around $4.5 million before the conflict, according to Michael Haigh, head of commodities research at Societe Generale.

The increased reliance on Hormuz comes as Saudi Arabia's alternative export routes remain constrained. The East-West Pipeline, which carries crude from the kingdom's eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, was shut down as a precaution after attacks in the Riyadh and Medina regions, the Saudi Press Agency said earlier this month. Saudi-flagged vessels have also stopped transiting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait following attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Saudi-linked shipping, while more than a dozen have rerouted around South Africa's Cape of Good Hope, according to maritime-intelligence firm Windward.
